text_fidelity_a:
KINESIS Freestyle2 USB Keyboard for Mac (9" Standard Separation), Black Overall this keyboard is great. The keys feel nice and they're quiet but not too quiet or soft or squishy. Enjoy typing on this keyboard, pushing the keys seems to take minimal effort and overall it's great.

The best part about the keyboard is that it separates and having the ability to give it a little separation is great. I miss it when I don't have it and it helps avoid torquing the wrists when you are typing. I also love the feel of the keys.

Now before my minor complaints understand two things: (1) I really like this keyboard and despite what I would consider minor defects, I would definitely buy another one. (2) please excuse the fact that I like my keyboards to be consistent and while Apple may not make the *best* keyboards I do use a laptop and I am used to their keyboard layout and feel.

The biggest thing that annoyed me when I purchased this keyboard was the positioning of the ⌘ (command) key. It seems to be shifted over a bit from what I'm used to. Normally I would hit ⌘ with my thumb but it's a little touch to do that on this one given the position of it. It's just something I'm having to get used to.

One minor downside to the keyboard is that the function key doesn't work the same way as the default apple keyboard, rather, the `fn` key is a toggle. I prefer for fn to work as a modifier because that is what I am used to on my laptop keyboard.

Another minor problem is the styling on the caps lock key. Like many people, I remap my caps lock to ctrl and and thus want caps lock to be a normal button. However, on this keyboard the caps lock key is missing the right part of the key so that you don't accidentally hit it when typing the `a` key.

Finally, the escape key and '`' (back tick) keys are in weird positions. The escape key is not as bad as the backtick. There is just something about the distance that I must go that is different from what I'm used to and I have been consistently hitting the `1` key instead. Life goes on.
text_fidelity_b: KINESIS Freestyle2 USB Keyboard for Mac (9" Standard Separation), Black

text_fidelity_a:
TiVo Roamio OTA 1 TB DVR - With No Monthly Service Fees - Digital Video Recorder and Streaming Media Player Overall it works well. And I love the no-monthly fee part of this unit. Though the unit runs slowly, as if it runs on a 1990-circa CPU.

The setup was super easy and straight forward. Picked up about 70 channels in the Denver market. (Didn't know there were that many.) Though half of them didn't actually broadcast anything. Then I had to narrow it down to about 10 channels that broadcast meaningful contents. It took a long time to download and apply updates during the initial setup. Took about 2 hours.

The menu navigates slowly. Each action took about 3-5 seconds for the unit to finish. The OnePass makes recording a series far more complicated than necessary. I have to jump through many hoops to make it happen. On my cable remote, I can simply press the record button twice to setup a series recording.

I really like how seamlessly TiVo integrates with my Netflix, Amazon Prime and Youtube accounts and leads me directly to the episodes. It is very convenient to use and it's quite a pleasant surprise.

My only gripe is when I view a recorded program and navigate the menu, I cannot exit the menu to go back to full screen viewing of my recorded program. The "back" button only backs out to the main menu. So I have to select the recorded program and resume viewing. For live TV, I can simply click on the "Live TV" button to go back to full screen viewing.

Despite its imperfection, the TiVo with no monthly fee is an outstanding value. For those who are looking to cut the cable or ditch the dish, this is the way to go.

[Update 2017.01.24] Downgrading from 5 to 3 stars. TiVo is supposed to do periodic updates only overnight, but two Sundays in a row, the unit attempted to perform updates during the day. The first update froze the unit so we missed 3 quarters of a NFL playoff game. The second time we caught it in time, so only missed a few minutes of another playoff game.
text_fidelity_b: TiVo Roamio OTA 1 TB DVR - With No Monthly Service Fees - Digital Video Recorder and Streaming Media Player

text_fidelity_a:
CHUWI Hi8 8 inch Windows 10/Android 4.4 Dual Boot Tablet PC, with Features of Intel Quad Core, Full HD 19201200 IPS Screen, 2G RAM/32G ROM and Winkey Price is one thing that's good about this tablet. I have no problem with the cheap plastic all around (really, it almost felt like a disposable food tray), considering the price tag, but there were a couple of things I just couldn't get over.

- Whatever Android OS is installed here, it came without Google Play app. Once I installed it myself, it crashed every time I tried to download a new app from Google app store. This is unacceptable, especially considering that the tablet comes with almost no apps to begin with.
-By the time I updated Windows & set up tablet, it was already getting uncomfortable warm. I can't imagine what would happen if I tried doing something like taping a video for an hour.
- USB socket was loose, I had to jiggle the cable several times to get it charging, and a smallest shift caused it to disconnect again.
- I expected pretty poor camera from the specs, but this was outstanding. Video & images had all the charm and quality of those tiny snapshots from the early mobile phones. Made me kind of nostalgic, but I expect better from a current tablet.

Unrelatedly to the quality of tablet itself, I'm glad I got to try a Windows 10 OS tablet on a dual boot machine, so I know to avoid it from now on... a clumsy hybrid of desktop and tablet capabilities. Android booted and run reasonably fast, while Win 10 lagged on the same machine.

I'm returning it.
text_fidelity_b: CHUWI Hi8 8 inch Windows 10/Android 4.4 Dual Boot Tablet PC, with Features of Intel Quad Core, Full HD 19201200 IPS Screen, 2G RAM/32G ROM and Winkey

Worth noting is that the case seems very thin around the drive, which is probably good for heat dispersion, but will not provide the kind of protection you'd want if you were constantly transporting this drive.

I now have on here hundreds of seasons of TV shows, most in HD, nearly a thousand movies, most in HD, hundreds of music albums, books, maps, comics, software setup files, etc., and I STILL have room to grow. To get all these things consolidated and organized - and all accessible with a single drive powered up - is really fantastic.

text_fidelity_a:
Fujifilm FinePix Z90 14 MP Digital Camera with Fujinon 5x Wide Angle Optical Zoom Lens and 3-Inch Touch-Screen LCD (Red) This camera is what I call a "subcompact" - the smallest point and shoot cameras that have vertically mounted lenses which allow protection, compactness, and quicker start up times. Normally, you'd expect a small trade off for these features, so I wouldn't compare this directly with a camera endowed by a telescoping lens.

Sony invented the subcompact with the T1 a few years back (at least in my world), and I was able to compare the FinePix Z90 with the one-generation-older 12 MP Sony T90. I'll go the pro/con route...

PROS of the Z90:

-Price is something like half of the latest subcompact Sony.
-Operational costs are cheaper: USB cable is non-proprietary (in case you want a second one or need to replace it) and SD card is cheaper and more universal than Sony's Memory Stick.
-Separate physical buttons to record movies and to take pictures. This is genius to me, because I hate to miss a great video opportunity while fumbling through the menus.
-Does not come with a memory card, BUT cameras that do usually come with one so small that it is worthless. Internal memory is better, because it allows you to copy from one camera card to another, which can be useful.
-Can set it up to take two photos at once, with and without the flash. As an amateur, I often do this manually anyway, but this way you get closer photos (chronologically)to compare in a dynamic scenario, and the subject needs only to pose once.
-The panorama mode works better than in other cameras I've used. They use internal weights alla smart phones (I'm guessing) to help you line up the next picture. Allows you to "pan" a panorama shot in play mode.
-There is a time zone mode that allows you to temporarily change the time (for timestamps).
-The display changes from horizontal to vertical as you move the camera respectively.
-"Touch and track" mode follows a subject.
-Side by side picture compare.
-Search by face, couple, group, favorites, scene, or date, and view a small picture next to thumbnails.
-Charger is smaller with the plug offset to allow it to use only one receptacle on a power strip (as long as it is at the end of said strip).

CONS of the Z90:

-Picture quality was not as good as the Sony 80% of the time (tested in various modes and lighting conditions). That said, a tripod really helps with low light and no flash, where both cameras struggle without it.
-By numbers, it is not much larger than the Sony, but it feels significantly larger.
-Sometimes the "buttons" in the corners of the touch screen need to be pressed more than once.
-Tripod mount has plastic threads, instead of a machined metal insert.
-Cannot take shots as rapidly as on the Sony
-Does not tell you what zoom level you are at. 5x zoom does not appear to make a great difference over 4x.
-"play" and "camera" buttons could be one button used as a toggle.
-Battery can be put in backward, as the slot is not keyed (although the battery is). No big deal, but shows something wasn't thought out thoroughly.

Bottom Line:

The Fuji is trying to deliver everything the market leader has to offer for a much more manageable price tag. It gets an A for effort, delivering a lot of great menu options, and may actually win in that respect, but the picture quality is not as good. If they could pour a little more money into the actual optics and the touch screen and still keep the price reasonable, they might win the battle in the future. For now, it's purely a personal budget vs. quality decision.
text_fidelity_b: Fujifilm FinePix Z90 14 MP Digital Camera with Fujinon 5x Wide Angle Optical Zoom Lens and 3-Inch Touch-Screen LCD (Red)

text_fidelity_a:
Epson ProSense 347 GPS Multisport Watch with Heart Rate and Ultra Long Battery Life - Black I've been testing this Epson ProSense watch for the past week. I also have a 2-year-old Garmin Vivoactive HR watch that has most of the same features, but costs half as much. To the compare the two, I've been wearing one watch on each wrist and going on runs and bike rides to see how their readings compare. Both watches have daily step counters that give similar results (today, Garmin says 12044 steps while Epson says 12790 steps). 5% difference is close enough for me.

When I use the GPS exercise mode, the results start showing big differences. On today's run, Garmin recorded 4.02 miles while Epson says 3.9 miles. That's a 3% difference which is close enough for me. Garmin says 529 calories and Epson says 955 calories. Garmin says 535 feet of elevation gain and Epson says 1142 feet. I know Garmin has a barometric altimeter, while Epson is using GPS elevation, which is notoriously inaccurate. Does Epson's terrible elevation data cause a wildly inaccurate calorie count? I could not find any information on Epson's calorie calculation in their documentation, so I really cannot trust it.

Both devices give me heart rate readings with graphs by time or broken out by training zones. The numbers look close enough for my purposes. Both devices also give me maps of my route, which is is nice to have for reviewing later, especially if it is a new route to me.

The Epson is a much larger device (both width and thickness), as shown in the photo. While the Garmin is not especially attractive, at least it is relatively unobtrusive. Epson is big enough to feel clunky on my wrist, especially if I am wearing it all day (to take advantage of the step counter).

Both devices have a smartphone app that syncs your data and also sends notifications to the watch. I'm using this watch with a Google Pixel Android phone. The Garmin app by default uploads your data to the Garmin website. With Epson, you have to upload to a 3rd party website like Strava, which may not be compatible with all the data that your device is collecting.

Notifications work much better with Garmin than Epson. For incoming phone calls, both Garmin and Epson will display the caller ID or contact name so I don't have to pull out my phone to see who is calling. For incoming emails, Garmin displays the sender name and subject line, while Epson just says "you have mail". For text messages, Garmin shows the contact name and message. Epson shows no notification for text messages.

The only advantage (for my use case) that I can find with this Epson watch is the much longer battery life. Garmin claims 1 week of battery life with the GPS off or 13 hours with the GPS on. Epson claims 46 hours of battery life with the GPS on, which I suppose is great for some ultra endurance sports. For me, I never exercise more than 8 hours in a day.
text_fidelity_b: Epson ProSense 347 GPS Multisport Watch with Heart Rate and Ultra Long Battery Life - Black

text_fidelity_a:
TP-Link N300 Wireless Portable Nano Travel Router(TL-WR802N) - WiFi Bridge/Range Extender/Access Point/Client Modes, Mobile in Pocket I purchased this to try and create my own wireless network within a hospital room I would be in for a while. The problem as many have stated is most commercial WiFi system require you log into a splash page after you connect to their network. This router does not have a way to do that. You can try using one of your devices and then clone the MAC address to the router, but this only works if this router is connected to the network with the Ethernet cable port. Most hotels and hospitals no longer have working Ethernet jacks in rooms. If you try and clone the MAC address on the wireless port it creates a conflict and everything stops working.

So to sum up, it works fine as a cheap travel router, but if you have to deal with a splash page on an WiFi only network, it simply will not work. It can’t be that hard to create one of these with a built in browser for splash pages. Anyone listening????
text_fidelity_b: TP-Link N300 Wireless Portable Nano Travel Router(TL-WR802N) - WiFi Bridge/Range Extender/Access Point/Client Modes, Mobile in Pocket

Tech2 Three Sided Surge Protector Cube with 3 Outlets & USB Ports (Smart 3A Total) ETL Certified Adapter for Home, School, or Office This surge protector cube from Tech2 is great! It’s compact but has 3 AC outlets and 3 USB ports. The latter is especially useful since so many devices don’t include wall adapters anymore.

The output for the USB ports is 5V, 3A Max.

The USB ports glow blue whether you use them or not. The blue light is bright during the day and night, and can be seen even when there is a cable plugged into a port. I like and don’t like the illumination. It’s helpful at night if I need to plug something in, but then, the light is very bright in a dark room.

The cube doesn’t block the outlet below it, which I also like. If plugged into the bottom outlet on a normal wall socket, it will block the top outlet.

I like the small size, it’s great for keeping in your bag in case you need a bunch of outlets. But it’s also functional at home, and has replaced one of my bulky power strips.

The surge protector is made in China.
